fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The Pharisees ask, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?" (Matthew 19:3). Pharisees were a strict religious group, and Matthew says they came to test Him. So this question came as a test.

Good guess, friend, because taxes did come up in a test question on another day. That's Matthew 22:16–17, when the Pharisees send their disciples along with the Herodians to ask whether it's lawful to pay the census tax to Caesar, the Roman emperor. Here in chapter 19, though, the test is about divorce. The question is whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason (Matthew 19:3).

David was a great king, no doubt about it. But Jesus isn't pointing to a throne here. He says "…from the beginning…" which goes back to when the Creator "made them male and female…" (Matthew 19:4). David shows up many, many chapters later, when he becomes king over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3).

I get why it sounds nice, friend, but it's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart." (Matthew 19:8). So the word is hardness, not purity. Purity would have been a much prettier word, but it isn't the one Jesus uses.

Gladness is a lovely word, but it doesn't fit this verse. Jesus says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart." (Matthew 19:8). I think that's a heavy line. The right word is hardness.

That's right, baker. His disciples say, "If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry." (Matthew 19:10). I think Jesus's teaching hit them hard. I bet they were stunned, and honestly, I'd have been staring at my apron too.

The temple was the center of worship in Jerusalem, so I see why you picked it (2 Chronicles 6:6). But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says some live like eunuchs "…for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 19:12). The temple never comes up in this passage.

Close, because the people bringing them did the work of getting the children to Jesus. But Jesus says, "For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." (Matthew 19:14). He's pointing at the children themselves. The ones bringing them aren't the ones He names.

That's right, baker. Matthew says, "And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there." (Matthew 19:15). The children were brought for Him to place His hands on them (Matthew 19:13), and He did. The disciples' scolding didn't get the last word.

This one is true, friend. Matthew says, "And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there." (Matthew 19:15). The people brought the children so Jesus could place His hands on them (Matthew 19:13). He did, and then He moved on.
